title: Rules
subtitle: How Wazuh and Suricata each decide what becomes an alert — and how to write, apply, and verify a new rule in each one.

intro.text: Two custom rules in Wazuh (100101 and 100200) and one custom signature in Suricata (sid 9000001) carry most of the detection in this lab. This page brings together, in one place, how each engine decides what becomes an alert, the real step-by-step for writing a new rule in each, and how to verify afterward — both in the dashboard and on the command line — that it actually loaded.

intro.title: Why this page exists separately from the Wazuh page
intro.text: The Wazuh page already covers the full investigation behind each rule: why 100200 exists, the 90-second timing bug, the port-scan detection gap. This page is the opposite — a straight reference guide, no investigation narrative, for when all that's needed is a reminder of "how do I add a new rule" without rereading everything.

sections.title: How rules work: two different engines

blocks.text: The lab runs two completely separate detection engines, and each decides "this is an alert" in a different way:

rows: What it looks at
Logs and events already collected from agents — FIM, auditd, Windows Event Log, even Suricata's own eve.json
Raw network packets, captured live on each sensor's interface
When it decides
After the event was already generated by another source (syscheckd, auditd, etc.)
In real time, directly on traffic crossing the interface
Where rules live
A single central file on the manager: /var/ossec/etc/rules/local_rules.xml
A separate local.rules file on each individual sensor
Syntax
XML
One text line per signature, Snort-style

blocks.title: The gotcha that trips everyone up once
blocks.text: A Suricata alert (like the port scan one) does not become its own rule inside Wazuh — it comes in through the generic rule 86601, which wraps ANY alert coming from eve.json. The actual signature text lives inside the alert itself, in the data.alert.signature field, not in rule 86601's description. That's why the port scan signature never shows up on Wazuh's "Rules" screen, only the generic 86601.
The two real rules in this lab cover the two valid ways to filter an event — by structured field, or by free text:

blocks.code:
<group name="local,media_isolation,">
  <rule id="100200" level="12">
    <if_sid>550,553,554</if_sid>
    <field name="file">^/srv/media</field>
    <description>Media storage node: file integrity change detected in /srv/media (possible ransomware behavior)</description>
    <group>media_isolation,</group>
  </rule>
</group>

blocks.text: This correlates three FIM rules Wazuh already ships (550 modified, 553 deleted, 554 added) and restricts them to only fire when the structured file field matches the protected path — filtering by <field>.

blocks.code:
<rule id="100101" level="3">
  <if_sid>86601</if_sid>
  <match>Ethertype unknown</match>
  <description>Suricata: Ethertype unknown - downgraded (known noise from home network IoT devices)</description>
  <group>suricata_tuning,</group>
</rule>

blocks.text: This one branches off the generic rule for any Suricata alert (86601) and looks for free text anywhere in the log — filtering by <match>. Opposite direction from 100200: instead of escalating, it downgrades the severity of an already-identified noise pattern.
The parts that matter

items: id — above 100000; that range is reserved for custom rules, below it is Wazuh's factory ruleset.
level — 0 to 16, decides severity; level 12+ tends to be what triggers Active Response in this lab.
if_sid — chains off an existing rule (e.g. 550/553/554 are the built-in generic FIM rules).
field vs match — field uses a structured field of the event (e.g. the file path); match looks for free text anywhere in the log.
group — the tag that later ties the rule to a dashboard, a saved query, or an Active Response condition.

sections.title: How to add a new rule in Wazuh

blocks.text: Real step-by-step, run directly on soc-server (where the manager lives):

items: Back up the file before touching it.
Pick a free ID and confirm it doesn't already exist.
Edit as root.
Always add the new rule at the end of the file, inside its own <group>...</group> block — never insert via automated find-and-replace.
Save and restart the manager.
Wait for the engine to actually finish reloading before testing.

blocks.code:
sudo cp /var/ossec/etc/rules/local_rules.xml /var/ossec/etc/rules/local_rules.xml.bak
grep -c 'id="100201"' /var/ossec/etc/rules/local_rules.xml   # confirm the ID is free
sudo nano /var/ossec/etc/rules/local_rules.xml
sudo systemctl restart wazuh-manager

blocks.title: The 90-second lesson that once cost a full day of debugging
blocks.text: On this lab's 2-core hardware, the rule engine takes up to 90 seconds to fully reload after a systemctl restart wazuh-manager. Testing before that window passes gives the false impression of "this rule doesn't work" — it was mistaken for a syntax bug for most of a day once.

blocks.title: Why never edit via script/automated replace
blocks.text: A str.replace() targeting </group> can silently hit the wrong nested group tag and corrupt the whole file with no warning — this happened twice in this lab. Edit manually, or always append at the end of the file.
Validating before trusting it

items: Log-line-based rule (e.g. sshd, sudo): sudo /var/ossec/bin/wazuh-logtest, paste a sample log line, confirm it matches the expected ID.
No log line to simulate (FIM, rootcheck): trigger the real event (e.g. edit a file on the monitored path) and check Threat Hunting.

sections.title: How to view rules in Wazuh

blocks.text: Two ways to confirm a rule is loaded and working: through the dashboard, or directly on the command line.
In the dashboard

items: Server Management → Rules.
Click "Custom rules" (top right) to filter down to only the rules you wrote, without the thousands of factory rules mixed in.
Or use free-text search: by ID (100200), by group (media_isolation), or by a word from the description.

blocks.title: Don't confuse the "example rule" with "your rule"
blocks.text: Every freshly installed local_rules.xml ships with a factory example rule (ID 100001, "sshd: authentication failed from IP 1.1.1.1"). It shows up in the "Custom rules" filter too, but it was never written or used on purpose — worth knowing how to tell it apart from what's actually yours.
Seeing the rule actually fire (Threat Hunting / Discover)
On the command line, directly on soc-server
Unlike Wazuh's XML, a Suricata signature is a single line of text, Snort-style syntax. The only custom rule in this lab — the port scan detector, replicated across all 8 sensors:

blocks.code: alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"LOCAL Possible TCP Port Scan Detected"; flags:S; threshold: type both, track by_src, count 20, seconds 60; classtype:attempted-recon; sid:9000001; rev:1;)

blocks.text: The parts that matter

items: action — alert (logs to eve.json) is the only one used here; drop/reject also exist for inline-blocking setups, not used in this lab.
protocol and addresses — tcp any any -> $HOME_NET any: any source, any port, against the local network, any destination port.
options in parentheses — msg is the text that shows up as data.alert.signature in Wazuh; flags:S restricts to SYN packets only; threshold is the real trick (see below).
sid — must be unique; Suricata/Snort convention itself reserves sid above 1,000,000 for local/custom rules (the ET Open ruleset uses the range below that).
classtype / rev — category and revision metadata, doesn't change whether the rule fires.

blocks.title: threshold is what separates "useful rule" from "rule that fills the disk"
blocks.text: Without threshold, a 1000-port SYN scan would generate 1000 near-identical alerts within seconds. "type both, track by_src, count 20, seconds 60" collapses all of that into a single alert line per 60-second window, per source IP.

sections.title: How to add a new rule in Suricata

blocks.text: Unlike Wazuh, there's no single central file here — each of the 8 sensors has its own local.rules, and a new rule only protects the machine where it was manually replicated.

items: Confirm the actual rules file path on that specific machine — it isn't always the same: /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules on most, but /var/lib/suricata/rules/local.rules on tales-desktop (default-rule-path shifts depending on the Suricata version/install method).
Write the signature line into local.rules.
Make sure local.rules is listed under rule-files: inside suricata.yaml — if the file exists on disk but isn't in that list, it's silently ignored, with no error.
Validate the syntax BEFORE restarting the service.
Restart the service — the right mechanism depends on the operating system.

blocks.code:
sudo nano /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules
sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml -v   # look for "0 rule files failed"
sudo systemctl restart suricata                       # Linux

rows: Linux (4 sensors)
sudo systemctl restart suricata — the straightforward path, no gotchas.
Windows (2 sensors)
The native service (--service-install) dies on its own seconds after starting. A Task Scheduler entry is used instead (AtStartup, SYSTEM) — Stop-ScheduledTask + Start-ScheduledTask to recycle it.
macOS (1 sensor)
No brew services support — supervised via LaunchDaemon: sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.oisf.suricata.

blocks.title: Repeat it on every sensor, not just one
blocks.text: A new rule written only in victim-linux's local.rules doesn't protect tales-desktop or any other sensor — the same text (adjusting the path if needed) has to be manually replicated across all 8 sensors, one by one.

sections.title: How to view rules in Suricata

blocks.text: Directly on the sensor — the source of truth

blocks.code:
cat /etc/suricata/rules/local.rules
# or, if the path is different on that machine:
cat /var/lib/suricata/rules/local.rules

blocks.text: This is the only place where the full rule text (threshold, flags, sid) is actually visible. Wazuh never shows this text — only the result of when it fires.
Through Wazuh, by looking at the alerts it already generated
Since there's no dedicated "Rules" screen for Suricata inside Wazuh, the path is to look at alerts already fired in Discover/Threat Hunting:

blocks.title: Discovering signatures without knowing the exact name
blocks.text: Clicking the data.alert.signature field in Discover's left-hand field list shows the "Top 5 values" for that field over the selected period — the fastest way to find out which signatures (including your own custom ones) have already fired, without guessing the name first.

rows: Rule file
/var/ossec/etc/rules/local_rules.xml (central, one on the manager)
local.rules (per sensor, path can vary by machine)
ID range reserved for custom rules
sid above 1,000,000
Validate syntax before applying
wazuh-logtest, or trigger the real event for rules with no log line
suricata -T -c suricata.yaml -v
Apply the change
systemctl restart wazuh-manager (~90s reload on this hardware)
Varies by OS: systemctl (Linux), Task Scheduler (Windows), LaunchDaemon (macOS)
Where to view it in the Wazuh dashboard
Server Management → Rules → "Custom rules" button
No dedicated screen — shows up via generic rule 86601, real text in the data.alert.signature field
Where to view it on the command line
grep in local_rules.xml
cat local.rules on each sensor, one by one
